reason: The sources support over 10 claims backed by multiple independent sites detailing Amundsen's secret plans, execution, and success.
story: In 1910, Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen set sail on the Fram, telling his crew they were heading to the Arctic. In secret, he redirected the ship to Antarctica after learning American rivals had claimed the North Pole. Amundsen established a base camp at the Bay of Whales and planned a rapid assault on the South Pole using Greenland sled dogs and skis. In October 1911, five men and 52 dogs embarked on the final march. To traverse the punishing terrain and high mountain glaciers, Amundsen systematically slaughtered weaker dogs at a camp dubbed the Butchers' Shop, feeding their meat to the surviving dogs and men. On December 14, 1911, Amundsen's team reached the South Pole, planting the Norwegian flag five weeks before British rival Robert Falcon Scott. Amundsen returned safely with just 11 surviving dogs, completing history's most ruthless and successful polar race.
angle: To beat his British rival to the South Pole, Roald Amundsen systematically slaughtered his own sled dogs along the march to feed his men and remaining canine teams.

claims.claim: Roald Amundsen led the Norwegian expedition that became the first to reach the Geographic South Pole on December 14, 1911.
Amundsen originally planned an expedition to the North Pole, but pivoted south after learning American explorers claimed to have reached the North Pole.
Amundsen kept his change of destination secret from the public, his backers, and most of his crew when setting sail in 1910.
Amundsen revealed the true Antarctic destination to his crew after leaving Madeira in September 1910.
Amundsen sent a telegram to British explorer Robert Falcon Scott informing him that the Fram was proceeding to Antarctica.
Amundsen built his Antarctic base camp, Framheim, at the Bay of Whales on the Ross Ice Shelf.
The expedition sailed aboard the Fram, a polar research vessel originally constructed for Fridtjof Nansen's Arctic drift.
Amundsen's initial attempt to march south in September 1911 failed and was forced back to base camp due to extreme cold.
The final South Pole journey began in October 1911 with a five-man team using four sledges and 52 Greenland sled dogs.
At the summit of the Axel Heiberg Glacier, the team slaughtered excess dogs at a location named the Butchers' Shop, feeding the meat to the men and surviving dogs.
Amundsen's team reached the South Pole roughly five weeks ahead of Scott's party.
At the South Pole, Amundsen's team pitched a tent named Polheim and left a letter addressed to King Haakon VII of Norway.
Only 11 of the 52 sled dogs survived the entire 99-day journey to the South Pole and back to base camp.
Captain Robert Falcon Scott and his four companions reached the pole after Amundsen but perished on their return trek.

disputed: The exact departure date of the final South Pole trek (October 19 vs October 20, 1911): attribute 'according to one account' or state mid-October 1911.
The exact number of dogs killed at the glacier summit (24 vs 27): leave out the exact slaughter count or state roughly two dozen.
Primary cause of Scott's failure (harsh conditions and man-hauling vs base camp officers disobeying orders): leave out base camp blame controversy or attribute 'according to a recent study'.
